churchward-lost-continent-mu-1926:

defoe-history-of-the-devil-1726:

black-tertiary-man-asia-choukoutien-1926:

livy-history-rome-books-9-26:

fortune-secrets-of-dr-taverner-1926:
Doctor Taverner heals minds by means no common clinic knows, in Dion Fortune's tales of 1926. The Secrets of Dr. Taverner gathers her occult detective stories in one book. A young doctor tells the cases of his strange chief, case by case.

Each tale turns on a haunting, a curse, a past life, or a soul out of place, solved by Taverner's art. Fortune drew on her nursing years and her occult work alike. The tales teach her ideas while they thrill and chill the reader. The book founded the psychic doctor line of occult fiction.
tombazi-photographic-expedition-kangchen:
Nicholas Tombazi took a camera to the glaciers of Kangchenjunga and came back with a tale for the ages. His Account of a Photographic Expedition to the Southern Glaciers appeared in 1926. In it he tells what he saw on the Sikkim side in 1925.

At 15,500 feet he watched a wild man, as he took it, moving on the slope below him. He tells of the form, the gait, and the measured footprints left in the snow. His is the most detailed early yeti report from a trained observer. The book anchors the whole shelf of yeti lore.
dunsany-charwomans-shadow-1926:
Dunsany turned to comedy in The Charwoman's Shadow, his novel of 1926. A young lord trades his shadow to a magician for gold to win his love. The lighter twin of the Elfland book, it completes his great fantasy run of the 1920s.

The lost shadow draws the hero into a Spain of enchantment, bandits, and a scheming mage. A charwoman's own shadow holds a key to the cure, as the title hints. The book charms where its mate awed, and its wit is warm. It shows Dunsany could laugh in the worlds he made grave.
mirrlees-lud-in-the-mist-1926:
Hope Mirrlees set a prim town by the edge of faerie in Lud-in-the-Mist, her novel of 1926. The town bans all talk of fairy fruit and the wild hills. Yet the fruit slips in. Sons and girls stray, and old rites stir in the calm streets.

The tale blends law, lore, and quiet dread. Mirrlees writes with grace and sly wit. She asks what a town loses when it shuts out awe. The book was long hard to find. Now chief tale-smiths rank it at the top. Mayor Chanticleer, stiff and prim at first, must face his own past. His slow change gives the wild lore a warm, sad human core.
toland-celtic-religion-druids-1726:
John Toland was an Irish free thinker. He wrote this study of Celtic faith and learning late in life, and it came out in 1726, after his death. The text here is from the 1815 printing. Toland was known for bold views on faith and church power.

He treated the druids as men of their time, not as priests of dark rites. With a cool eye he sifted old Greek and Roman reports from Welsh and Irish lore. His book was the first clear, sharp account of the druids in the age of reason.
mcbride-symmes-theory-concentric-spheres:
James McBride, a friend and backer of Symmes in Ohio, gave the hollow earth scheme its first full book in 1826. Symmes had put his claim in short forms, and it drew much scorn. McBride set out to give it a learned, full dress case.

He lays out the spheres within spheres, the polar holes, and the seas and lands inside. He draws on maths, star lore, and the tales of north sea men for his proof. The book is the chief shield of the scheme in its first, bold years.
summers-history-witchcraft-1926:
Montague Summers was a Catholic priest and a firm foe of witchcraft. His History of Witchcraft and Demonology came out in 1926. Summers held, as few of his day did, that the witch cult was real. His book tells the tale with vast stores of fact.

Pacts with the Devil, sabbats, and spells fill the early parts. The great trials of Europe and the New World take up the rest. Summers cites trial rolls, old tracts, and church law in bulk. The book is a mine of tales, read best with a keen eye on its slant.
doyle-land-of-mist-1926:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote The Land of Mist in 1926. Doyle gave his last years to the spirit creed and its cause. The tale brings back Professor Challenger, now old and fierce in grief. His child Enid and a young news man lead the tale's probe.

Seances, spirit guides, and tales of the dead fill the crew's path. Challenger fights the creed at first, then falls to its proofs one by one. Doyle meant the tale as a plea for faith in life past death. It is his clear creed told in the dress of a tale.
bible-tyndale-new-testament-1526:
William Tyndale put the New Testament into English and saw it printed in 1526, the first printed English New Testament. He worked from Greek, not Latin, and paid for the work with exile. Church leaders banned his text, yet copies spread fast across England.

Readers get the four Gospels, Acts, the letters of Paul and others, and Revelation. Tyndale wrote in plain, strong English that later Bibles kept. Much of the King James wording starts here. His version changed how English people read Scripture and how English prose sounds. Its cadence rings through church and school to this day.
swift-gullivers-travels-1726:
Jonathan Swift published Gulliver's Travels in 1726, in the first edition text used here. The full title sends Gulliver into several remote nations of the world. Readers took it first as a true travel tale, then as fierce satire.

Gulliver visits Lilliput, where men are six inches tall and wars turn on eggs. In Brobdingnag he is tiny, and a huge king scorns England's pride and guns. Later trips reach a flying island and the wise horse Houyhnhnms and brutish Yahoos. Man looks worse at each stop, and pride takes the hardest knocks of all. Swift's prose stays cool while the charges grow more and more savage.
hemingway-sun-also-rises-1926:
Ernest Hemingway published The Sun Also Rises in 1926, his novel of Jake Barnes and the expatriates of Paris. The Lost Generation's founding document follows drifting expatriates from Paris cafés to the Pamplona fiesta. Hemingway drew the cast from his own circle, and the roman à clef gossip only fed the book's fame.

Jake, wounded in the war, loves Brett Ashley, who drifts through men she cannot settle with in Paris and Spain. The fishing at Burguete gives a brief peace before the fiesta's bullfights, wine, and brawls take over in Pamplona. Romero, the young bullfighter, restores a code of grace under pressure that the expatriates admire and nearly corrupt by contact. Hemingway's cut, plain sentences and dialogue that implies oceans made a style a generation copied. The book defined how America writes about war's aftermath and expatriate drift.
hughes-weary-blues-1926:
Langston Hughes published The Weary Blues in 1926, his first book of poems. Hughes was a young Black writer linked to the Harlem Renaissance. The poems draw on blues and jazz, with their rhythms, refrains, and plain speech. Harlem streets, clubs, and workers fill the pages.

Some poems sing of joy and music late into the night. Others speak of weariness, low pay, and dreams put off. Hughes writes in voices close to the people he describes. The title poem shows a piano player swaying as he sings of having nobody in the world. The book announced a major new voice in American poetry.
guiraldes-don-segundo-sombra-1926:
Ricardo Guiraldes published Don Segundo Sombra in 1926, an Argentine novel told by a boy who becomes a gaucho. The narrator leaves a dull town life to ride with Don Segundo, a quiet and skilled horseman. On the pampas they herd cattle, break horses, and face storms and fights. The boy learns the gaucho code by watching his mentor.

Don Segundo speaks little, yet his example teaches courage, patience, and loyalty. At the end, the boy inherits land and must leave the roaming life. The farewell is sad and dignified. The novel is a beloved portrait of a fading way of life in Argentina.
whitehead-religion-making-1926:
Alfred North Whitehead published Religion in the Making in 1926, based on his Lowell Lectures. Whitehead treats religion as a human response to a vision of truth. He traces religion from tribal rites and ritual to more rational, universal forms. Solitude, he argues, stands at the heart of mature faith.

He asks how religion can stay honest in an age of science. Dogmas, he says, are formulas that point beyond themselves and must not harden. The book became a source text for process theology. Whitehead links God to the lure toward value in the world. It is a brief, humane work of religious philosophy.
tawney-religion-capitalism-1926:
R. H. Tawney published Religion and the Rise of Capitalism in 1926, a classic of economic history. Tawney, an English historian and socialist, studies how Christian teaching met the new market world. Medieval bans on usury gave way as commerce grew. Puritan teaching, he argues, could both discipline greed and bless success.

The book is often called the English answer to Weber's Protestant ethic. Tawney writes with moral force and fine irony. He mourns a lost age when faith set limits on acquisition. His closing plea joins economics to ethics. The work remains a humane, learned critique of acquisitive society. It shaped British social thought for decades.
spengler-decline-west-vol-1-1926:
Oswald Spengler's The Decline of the West, Volume 1, appears in Charles Francis Atkinson's translation of 1926. Subtitled Form and Actuality, the volume states Spengler's bold scheme. Cultures, he argues, are organisms that pass through birth, growth, maturity, and decay. Each has its own soul and its own mathematics, art, and science.

The West, in his reading, has entered its late, hard phase of civilization. Spengler compares cultures side by side in vast tables of parallel ages. Critics call the method prophetic rather than scientific. The book was the most debated philosophy of history of its century. Atkinson's version carried the debate into English.
malinowski-crime-custom-1926:

Malinowski argues that law lives in daily duty, not in force from above. He shows that custom binds because people depend on each other and fear shame before their neighbors. Gifts, feasts, and duties form a web that no one can lightly break. The book founded the study of law in anthropology and still starts debates about rules without rulers.
defoe-political-history-of-the-devil-172:
Daniel Defoe, the novelist of Robinson Crusoe, published The Political History of the Devil in 1726. The book traces Satan's career from the Fall through the witchcraft panics of Defoe's own recent past. Defoe mocks credulous tales of pacts and apparitions while still treating the Devil as a real political schemer in human affairs. He sorts scripture, history, and street gossip with a journalist's nose for a weak story. The result reads like a skeptical sermon, funny and unsettling by turns.
cross-true-masonic-chart-1826:
Jeremy L Cross published The True Masonic Chart in 1826, and it became a well known American guide to lodge ritual. Cross was a traveling Masonic teacher who helped spread a shared form of work across many lodges. His chart used pictures as memory aids for members.

Rows of symbols, tools, and scenes, called hieroglyphic emblems, helped Masons recall the lessons of each degree. The text around them gave the order and sense of the ritual without printing every secret word. For historians, the chart shows how American Masonry taught itself, and how pictures carried meaning that words alone were not meant to hold.
barrett-besterman-divining-rod-1926:

Field tests, case reports, and past records fill the book, along with a study of how the rod moves. The authors looked for trickery, chance, and knowledge of the land that a dowser might not know he had. Their inquiry, among the last big SPR field studies, treats a folk craft with full scientific care.
arcandam-or-alcandrin-1626:

galsworthy-silver-spoon-1926:

Fleur, born with the silver spoon of the title, hunts for excitement and status in fashionable London. A libel case, a trip related to America, and clashes with her aging father test her marriage. Soames watches the new generation with worry and grudging love. The novel satirizes the smart set while keeping sympathy for its flawed people.
cummings-is-5-1926:
E. E. Cummings published is 5 in 1926, his second major collection of poems. By then his experiments with broken lines, scattered type, and lowercase letters were becoming famous. He divided the book into sections that move from satire to love poems.

The best-known piece here, anyone lived in a pretty how town, tells a whole life in a few musical, looping lines. Other poems mock politicians and professors, then soften into tender songs about lovers and seasons. Cummings plays with grammar the way jazz musicians play with rhythm. The collection shows him at his most beloved and most daring at once.
glasgow-romantic-comedians-1926:
Ellen Glasgow published The Romantic Comedians in 1926, her sharpest comedy of Southern manners. Glasgow set it in Richmond, renamed Queenborough, among the aging gentry she knew so well. She once described the book as a comedy about people who refuse to grow old gracefully.

Judge Gamaliel Honeywell, a widower of sixty-five, shocks his family by marrying a pretty young woman of twenty-three. The marriage collapses in farce and pathos, while his grown children pursue their own late romances. Glasgow mocks Southern gallantry with unusual lightness of touch. Under the comedy sits a serious theme: the danger of living inside romantic illusions. It remains one of her most entertaining novels.
hemingway-torrents-of-spring-1926:

cooper-last-of-the-mohicans-1826:

Captures, rescues, and massacres follow across glens and caverns Cooper made iconic. The title's tragedy gathers force as the old order of the forest dies with Uncas. faulkner-soldiers-pay-1926:
Soldiers' Pay, published in 1926, was the first novel of William Faulkner of Mississippi. Its central figure is Donald Mahon, a young flying officer badly wounded in the First World War. Scarred and nearly blind, Mahon comes home to a small Georgia town that does not know what to do with him.

Around the dying airman gather a kind widow, a cynical veteran, and Mahon's shallow fiancee. Each reacts to his ruin in a different way, from pity to flight. Faulkner writes in a lush, brooding style already marked by his later manner. The novel opened his long study of the South, war, and loss.
hurston-eatonville-anthology-1926:

Hurston treats the townsfolk with warmth and respect, never as mere curiosities. hurston-sweat-1926:
Sweat, a short story by Zora Neale Hurston, appeared in the magazine Fire in 1926. Its heroine is Delia Jones, a washerwoman in a Florida town. Delia has worked for years to buy her own house, while her lazy husband Sykes torments her and flaunts his mistress.

Sykes, knowing Delia fears snakes, brings home a rattlesnake to drive her out. The cruelty builds until the snake turns on its keeper. kafka-das-schloss-1926:

mathnawi-nicholson-vol-2-1926:
Jalal al-Din Rumi, the Persian poet of the 1200s, wrote the Mathnawi, a long poem of Sufi teaching told through stories. R. A. Nicholson spent years turning it into English. His second volume, printed in 1926, gives the English text of the poem's first two books.

Rumi teaches through tales of kings, lovers, merchants, fools, and saints, and each story turns toward a lesson on God and the soul. The tales pile up, short and long, comic and grave, and each one points past itself to truths about prayer, love, and the self. Nicholson's version became the standard English Mathnawi for students of Persian verse.
bailey-epicurus-extant-remains-1926:

His edition gives the Greek text with his own English version, along with notes and a critical apparatus.

Inside are three letters, to Herodotus, Pythocles, and Menoeceus, that sum up his physics and his ethics. Next come the Principal Doctrines, forty short sayings, and the Vatican Sayings, found in a single manuscript. Bailey's notes explain the hard points. For English readers of its day, this volume was the standard Epicurus.
llull-blanquerna-peers-1926:
Blanquerna is the great romance of Ramon Llull, the Catalan thinker of the thirteenth century. E. Allison Peers translated it into English in 1926. Its hero, Blanquerna, climbs step by step through the estates of the world: marriage, the religious life, the bishopric, the papacy, and at last the hermit's cell.

Along the road Llull sets out his whole vision of a reformed Christian world, taught by reason and his famous Art of finding truth. The famous Book of the Lover and the Beloved blooms inside the tale. Blanquerna is part novel, part plan for the church and the schools. It shows medieval Catalonia dreaming of a wiser age.
franck-kabbalah-sossnitz-1926:
Adolphe Franck, a French Jewish philosopher, published La Kabbale in 1843, the first modern critical history of Jewish mysticism. I. Sossnitz gave it English form in 1926, in a revised and enlarged edition. Franck wrote when scholars still treated the Kabbalah as a late fraud or a curiosity, and he took it seriously as philosophy.

He traces the Zohar and its doctrines of God, the sefirot, and the soul, and weighs its kinship with Plato, Philo, and the Gnostics. His calm method opened the field that Gershom Scholem would later rule. The book stays the gate through which the modern West entered the study of Kabbalah. Sossnitz brought Franck's French up to date for English readers.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-1:

The history was published in 1702 to 1704, after his death. Volume one here opens the Oxford edition of 1826, which runs to eight volumes.

Clarendon blends memoir with history: he knew the actors, sat in their councils, and weighed their characters. His portraits of the age's great men remain famous for their shrewdness and grace. The royalist cause has no fuller or finer advocate. Volume one begins the grandest English narrative of the civil wars.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-2:
Volume two continues Clarendon's History of the Rebellion in the Oxford edition of 1826. Edward Hyde wrote the history from his own years at the heart of royalist power, and it was published in 1702 to 1704. The work runs to eight volumes in this edition, each thick with council, camp, and character.

Clarendon's strength is the portrait: friend and foe alike stand forth as living men with mixed motives. He defends the king's cause while blaming royal errors with striking candor. The narrative carries the war's early campaigns in stately, rolling prose. For the inner story of Charles I's court at war, no source stands beside Clarendon. Volume two deepens that story.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-3:
The Oxford edition of Clarendon's History of the Rebellion reaches volume three of eight. Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, had served Charles I as chancellor and chief counselor before exile and disgrace. His history, published in 1702 to 1704, grew from notes and memory gathered across a lifetime in high politics.

Volume three holds the war's middle passage, where negotiation and battle chased each other year by year. Clarendon writes with a minister's grasp of paper, money, and men. His judgments on the great figures of the age shaped how later centuries saw them. The book is at once a royalist brief and a work of literature, and this volume keeps both alive.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-5:
Volume five continues the 1826 Oxford Clarendon, the History of the Rebellion and Civil Wars in England. Edward Hyde wrote the work across his years of power and exile, and it appeared in 1702 to 1704 in eight volumes in this edition. Few historians have written about events in which they played so large a part.

That nearness gives the narrative its weight: decisions of the king's council are told by a man who sat in it. Clarendon's measured prose hides strong feeling for the lost royalist cause. His character sketches, generous and severe by turns, remain models of the art. Volume five carries the war toward its end, with the council chamber always in view.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-6:
Clarendon's History of the Rebellion moves through volume six of the Oxford edition of 1826. Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, began the history during the war itself, at the urging of friends who saw it slipping into legend. The published work of 1702 to 1704 fills eight volumes in this edition.

The later volumes trace the royalist cause through defeat, exile, and the long wait for restoration. Clarendon never writes as a mere partisan: he scores his own side's blunders with care. His great gift, the lifelike portrait, stays sharp to the end. Readers meet the English Civil War here as tragedy told by a chief actor. Volume six keeps that telling grave and full.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-7:
Volume seven of the 1826 Oxford edition brings Clarendon's History of the Rebellion near its close. Edward Hyde wrote the history as the chief minister and counselor of Charles I, and its publication ran from 1702 to 1704. The eight-volume Oxford set is the classic form of the work.

In these later pages the war's outcome is sealed, and Clarendon turns to judgment: of men, of measures, of the causes that ruined a kingdom. His prose keeps its stately balance even in bitterness. No other royalist source matches his access to the king's mind and councils. Volume seven holds the penultimate share of the greatest memoir-history of the English civil wars.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-8:
Volume eight completes the Oxford edition of 1826 of Clarendon's History of the Rebellion and Civil Wars in England. Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, wrote the work from inside Charles I's council, and it was published in 1702 to 1704. Eight volumes hold the whole of his vast, personal history.

The closing volume ends the story of a kingdom torn apart and a cause lost and, in time, restored. Clarendon's portraits and judgments set the terms in which the civil wars were debated for two centuries. His book stands as the great royalist memoir-history, literary and documentary at once. To close volume eight is to finish the fullest inside account of England's great rebellion.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-4:
Volume four of Clarendon's History of the Rebellion follows the Oxford edition of 1826, though this volume comes from the 1827 printing of the same edition. Edward Hyde wrote the history from his place in Charles I's council, and it was published in 1702 to 1704 in eight volumes. The 1826 scan from Toronto could not be had, so the matched 1827 printing serves.

The fourth volume stands mid-war, where Clarendon's double gift shows best: narrative of events and portraits of the men who drove them. His account of the king's cause is partisan, learned, and deeply felt. No other royalist history matches its access or its art. The set reads whole with this volume in its proper place.
schleiermacher-soliloquies-1926:
Schleiermacher's Soliloquies, his Monologen of 1800, are a New Year gift the young thinker wrote for himself and his friends. Horace Leland Friess translated them for the Open Court edition of 1926. Friedrich Schleiermacher had just published his famous Speeches on Religion, and the Soliloquies turn the same searching mind inward.

The romantic self holds dialogue with itself on freedom, youth, aging, and the shape of a worthy life. Schleiermacher vows to stay true to his inner law against the world's pressure to conform. The prose glows with the ideals of his circle: friendship, love, and self-culture. Readers meet here the private voice of liberal theology's founder, thinking aloud.
engels-peasant-war-germany-olgin-1926:
Engels wrote The Peasant War in Germany in 1850, on the great revolt of 1525. Moissaye J. Olgin translated it for International Publishers in 1926. German peasants had risen against lords and princes three centuries earlier. Thomas Munzer, the radical preacher, leads the most daring wing in Engels's account.

Engels reads the revolt through class struggle, the first such Marxist history. Peasants, burghers, and nobles act from their place in the order of the day. Defeat, he argues, came from division among the rebels. The book set a pattern for Marxist history writing. It also rescued Munzer as a hero of the left. The narrative moves fast and hard.
tilden-toxemia-explained-1926:
John Henry Tilden blamed nearly all illness on one cause, and Toxemia Explained of 1926 states his case in full. Tilden, a Denver doctor who had turned against drug prescribing, taught that waste the body fails to clear poisons the blood. That state, toxemia, then shows itself as many different diseases.

Rest, fasting, and right living form his cure, since drugs only mask the warning signs. Tilden walks readers through digestion, habits, and the slow build-up of enervation, his word for drained nerve energy. The book became a classic of natural hygiene, and its plain, stern advice still finds readers.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol26:
The Journal of Discourses closes with Volume XXVI, printed at Liverpool in 1886 after more than thirty years. Twenty-six volumes hold sermons from 1854 onward, the longest such record of the Latter-day Saint movement ever made. Brigham Young's generation and its heirs speak across the whole run, caught in shorthand and fixed in print.

The final volume keeps the familiar form: doctrine, counsel, and defense from the senior elders of the church. With it, an archive ends that historians of American religion use daily, since nothing else preserves a faith's pulpit so fully. The set stands complete, a church's own voice across three decades.
holmes-science-of-mind-1926:
Ernest Holmes built a movement on The Science of Mind, whose first edition appeared in 1926. The thick textbook lays out a full course of lessons in what Holmes called Science of Mind and Spirit. Mind, in his teaching, responds to thought as law, and prayer becomes a treatment: a clear statement that heals.

Holmes drew on New Thought, scripture, and philosophy to frame Religious Science as both church and method. Lessons move from first principles to daily practice for health, supply, and peace. The 1926 text launched the Religious Science movement, and its churches still study this founding course.
radin-crashing-thunder-1926:
Crashing Thunder was a Winnebago (Ho-Chunk) man who told his life story to Paul Radin, who published it in 1926. Few books of the era let a Native American speak at such length in the first person about his own life.

He tells of his upbringing, his visions, his years of drinking and violence, and his turn to the peyote religion. His story moves through the Thunderbird clan's world of spirits, feasts, and obligations. Radin kept the telling close to the man's own voice and order. The result reads like a novel but is a real life, and it opened a new kind of native autobiography.
levy-bruhl-how-natives-think-1926:
Lucien Levy-Bruhl, a French philosopher, argued in this famous work that native peoples think in a fundamentally different way from modern Europeans. The authorized English translation by Lilian A. Clare appeared in 1926 and spread his thesis widely.

Levy-Bruhl claimed that collective representations, the beliefs a group shares, bend individual thought toward what he called participation mystique. In that mode, a person can feel one with an ancestor, an animal, or a sacred object. Critics attacked the idea as unfair to native reason, and Levy-Bruhl softened it late in life. The debate it started shaped anthropology for decades.
malinowski-myth-in-primitive-psychology-:
Malinowski based this short 1926 book on his fieldwork in the Trobriand Islands, where he had lived in a village and learned the language. It states his functionalist view of myth in its clearest form.

A myth, Malinowski argues, is not a bad attempt at science or history. It is a charter: a sacred story that justifies present customs, ranks, and land claims by grounding them in the age of origins. He shows Trobrianders using tales of ancestors to settle real disputes. The book helped move anthropology from the armchair to the field, and its argument still frames debates about myth.
lawrence-plumed-serpent-1926:
The Plumed Serpent, published in 1926, is Lawrence's Mexican novel and the most argued-over of all his books. Kate Leslie, an Irish widow of forty traveling in Mexico, is drawn into a movement reviving the cult of Quetzalcoatl, the plumed serpent god.

Its leaders, Don Ramon and Don Cipriano, preach a new-old religion of blood and ritual against church and revolution alike. Kate resists and yields by turns, and the novel never settles whether the cult saves or devours her. Lawrence wrote it out of his own Mexican journeys and longings. The result is powerful, disturbing, and impossible to ignore.
fitzgerald-all-sad-young-men-1926:
All the Sad Young Men, published in 1926, is Fitzgerald's third story collection, written at the height of his Jazz Age fame. Its title sets the tone: youth, money, and the sadness underneath both, in America after the war.

'The Rich Boy' studies a wealthy man whose money has deformed his capacity to love. 'Winter Dreams' follows Dexter Green's longing for Judy Jones and the world she stands for, and 'Absolution' turns to a boy and a priest in Minnesota. Fitzgerald's prose is at its most polished here, glamorous and quietly bleak. The stories remain his elegies for a generation.
cather-my-mortal-enemy-1926:
My Mortal Enemy, published in 1926, is Cather's short, pitiless novella of Myra Henshawe, remembered by a younger woman who knew her in youth and in ruin. Myra had given up a fortune to elope with Oswald Henshawe for love.

Years later the couple live poor and diminished, and Myra's bitterness turns on the man she chose. Her dying words name him her mortal enemy. Cather strips the elopement romance to the bone in barely a hundred pages. The late style here is bare, hard, and unforgettable, among the most perfect things she wrote in fiction.
ford-man-could-stand-up-1926:
A Man Could Stand Up, published in 1926, is the third volume of Ford's Parade's End. It opens on Armistice Day in London, the guns stopped at last, crowds half joyful and half lost, and Christopher Tietjens waiting in a silent office.

A telephone call from Valentine Wannop cuts through years of honor, pride, and paralysis, and Tietjens must finally choose his life. Around him, old scores are settled and the wartime world dissolves into parties and wreckage. Ford renders the day in rushing, broken impressions. The volume is the sequence's reckoning, long delayed and quietly immense.
smuts-holism-evolution-1926:
Holism and Evolution, published in 1926, is Jan Christiaan Smuts's philosophy of wholes. Smuts, the South African soldier-statesman, coined the word holism here for his claim that nature builds ever richer wholes, and that this building is evolution's deepest fact.

From matter to life to mind to personality, each level is a whole more than the sum of its parts, and mechanism cannot exhaust it. Smuts writes as a field naturalist and a statesman, not a laboratory man. The book influenced ecology and systems thought far beyond philosophy. Its vision of wholes remains its author's most original legacy.
morgan-theory-gene-1926:
Thomas Hunt Morgan led the famous 'fly room' at Columbia, where tiny fruit flies remade biology. His Theory of the Gene, published in 1926, sums up what those flies had taught. Morgan had once doubted Mendel; the flies changed his mind.

Morgan shows that genes sit in a line on chromosomes, like beads on a string. Crossed flies reveal how traits link, swap, and map to fixed places. That mapping let scientists chart heredity with real precision. Morgan won a Nobel Prize, and his book stands as the classic statement of gene theory. Diagrams of fly crosses make the argument easy to follow.
bernier-travels-mogul-empire-vol1-1826:
François Bernier, a French doctor, spent twelve years in India and served at the court of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb. Volume One of his Travels, in Brock's 1826 translation, reports what he saw between 1656 and 1668. It is the classic European account of Mughal India.

Bernier describes the war of succession among Shah Jahan's sons, the wealth of Delhi, and the habits of the court. He writes as a trained observer of medicine, trade, and religion. His letters home shaped how Europe pictured India for a century. Few early travelers match his mix of access and clear prose.
bernier-travels-mogul-empire-vol2-1826:
Volume Two of Bernier's Travels in the Mogul Empire continues his account of India under Aurangzeb. The French physician had traveled with the court and seen the empire at close range. Brock's translation completes the work in this volume.

The highlight is Bernier's trip to Kashmir with the emperor's camp, a rare early picture of that valley. He also writes on the Ganges delta, Hindu customs, and the burning of widows, which he condemns. His remarks on trade and land rent drew later thinkers on Asia. Together the two volumes remain a prime source on seventeenth-century India.
plos-pone-0003426:
Israel Hershkovitz and colleagues found ancient tuberculosis traces in this 2008 paper. They studied bones from a Neolithic settlement in the eastern Mediterranean. The settlement dated to about nine thousand years ago. Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the TB germ, was thought to have evolved beside humans for ages.

The team pulled out and characterized DNA of that germ from the remains. Finding it in such old bones backs the long shared history. TB leaves no home outside its human host, unlike many germs. This molecular proof pushes confirmed TB deep into prehistory. Few finds tie a named germ to a dated human settlement so directly.
plos-pone-0003526:
Lucina Q. Uddin and co-authors scanned self-face recognition in autism for this 2008 study. Autism involves less interest in social exchange and stronger self-focus. Earlier theories stressed social impairments in the disorder. The team asked how the brain handles self versus other faces.

Using brain imaging, they watched participants recognize their own faces. Neural patterns for self and other could then be compared. Where those patterns diverge may mark autism's social gap. The study gives a brain-level view of self representation. Face reading is core to social life, which is why its gaps matter.
plos-pone-0003626:
Elena R. Álvarez-Buylla, Álvaro Chaos, Maximino Aldana, and colleagues published this modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It asks how a flower takes shape as its genes switch on and off. The team built a model of the gene network that guides flower formation.

In their model, random noise could push the network toward stable flower forms, not just blur them. That runs against the older view of growth as a fixed, preset program. The study presents flower form as the product of a network that can use chance and still stay stable.
plos-pone-0003726:
Galit Tzur, Asaf Levy, Eti Meiri, and colleagues published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Human embryonic stem cells can renew themselves and can also turn into any body tissue. Small RNAs called microRNAs help steer that choice by tuning gene activity after genes are read.

The team tracked microRNA patterns as the cells differentiated toward endoderm, the layer that forms the gut and related organs. They also probed what those microRNAs do in the process. The patterns show small RNAs at work in one of the embryo's first big decisions.
plos-pone-0003826:
Daniel Mietchen, Bertram Manz, Frank Volke, and colleagues published this animal study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Below freezing, ice crystals threaten the structure and function of cells. Insects in seasonally cold places have evolved many strategies to reorganize their tissues against the cold.

The team assessed cold adaptation in insect larvae inside the living animal. They used magnetic resonance imaging and spectroscopy to watch tissues handle the cold without cutting them open. The in vivo view shows the tricks larvae use to survive deep cold through a hard winter. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008.
plos-pone-0003926:
Jianfeng Zhou, Wenhong Li, Hiroyasu Kamei, and co-authors compared a growth-control gene in fish in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns IGFBP-2, a protein that binds growth factors. It helps govern growth, development, reproduction, and aging. High levels of it also appear in many advancing cancers.

Teleost fish carry two copies of the gene, unlike most other vertebrates. The team compared the proteins those copies make and how each is used. Form and basic function stayed much the same after duplication. Gene use, though, had drifted apart between the two copies over time. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004026:
Francisco J. Quintana, Avishai Mimran, Pnina Carmi, and co-authors described a new immune control route in 2008. HSP60 is a heat shock protein that shapes T cell responses. It can signal through a receptor or serve as an antigen. The protein rises in stressed and inflamed tissues.

Their PLOS ONE article reports regulatory T cells target HSP60 itself. These anti-ergotypic cells react to the presented stress protein. That reaction forms another loop for calming immune responses. Understanding the loop may help treat autoimmune disease. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004126:
Kristin Field and colleagues published this feeding study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines casein hydrolysates, broken-down milk proteins used in foods for their nutrition and useful properties. Their bitter taste often limits how much makers can add to products meant for people.

Earlier evidence hinted that other animals also avoid eating them, but few species had been tested. The team offered animals a choice between foods with and without the hydrolysates. They found that plant-eating species avoided them, while omnivores did not. The result matters for food design and for understanding how taste guides diet across species.
plos-pone-0004226:
Yong Zhao and colleagues published this diabetes study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Type 1 diabetes is caused by the immune system destroying the pancreas's insulin-making beta cells. Controlling that autoimmunity is essential to any real treatment. Regulatory T cells, the immune system's peacekeepers, play a pivotal role in holding self-attack in check.

The team used human cord blood stem cells to modulate these regulatory T cells. They report that the treated cells reverse the autoimmune diabetes in nonobese diabetic mice, the standard model of the disease. The approach aims at the cause of type 1 diabetes, not just its blood sugar.
plos-pone-0004326:
Martin Schweizer, Markus Henniger, and Inge Sillaber published this stress study in PLOS ONE in 2009. In many depressed patients, stressful life events help trigger the illness. In rats, chronic mild stress can produce depression-like states, and the procedure is a standard animal model. Whether it works the same way in mice was less certain.

The team examined chronic mild stress in mice, looking at anhedonia, the loss of pleasure that is a core symptom, and at activity. They report an anomalous anxiolysis, a paradoxical calming, alongside the expected effects. Mixed results like these warn against assuming one species' model fits another.
plos-pone-0004426: In 2009, Andreotti, Minicuci, and Kowal profiled the whole world's health. Multidimensional health-status profiles from the WHO World Health Survey were carefully modeled. Seventy countries' wellbeing was compared head-to-head. The profiles guide global health policy today. The huge survey ran across three years.
plos-pone-0004526: In 2009, a Spanish team built a faster TB-vs-brucellosis test. Rapid differential diagnosis between the two diseases was developed. The quick DNA test split the tricky look-alikes. The tool aids hard-hit endemic regions today. The two diseases mimic each other almost exactly.
plos-pone-0004626: In 2009, Wagai, Senga, and Fegan tested whether doctors agree about sick kids anew. Agreement between rival clinicians assessing sick children was examined. The video-recorded cases were scored blind. The study informs treatment guidelines today. The doctor agreement varied widely.
plos-pone-0004726: In 2009, Chatterjee and Sarkar built a multi-step forecaster for malaria anew. A multi-step polynomial regression modeled and forecast malaria incidence. The causative factors were weighed carefully. The method aids public health planning today. The malaria problem is severe.
eichendorff-aus-dem-leben-eines-taugenic:
A miller's son with a fiddle, no money, and no plan walks out of his father's mill to seek his fortune. Eichendorff's Aus dem Leben eines Taugenichts, published in 1826 and given here in German, made that good-for-nothing the most beloved figure of German Romanticism. Adventures, mistaken identities, and romantic Italy crowd his road.

The Taugenichts drifts through gardens, castles, and a countess's household, lucky where others would starve. Poetry and song save him as often as wit does. Lazy, lyrical, and eternal, he embodies the Romantic hunger for the open road. No German book captures that wanderlust more perfectly. Readers have been packing his knapsack in their imaginations for two hundred years.
pero-tafur-travels-letts-1926:
Pero Tafur was a Castilian knight who roamed the late medieval world. His Travels and Adventures cover the years 1435 to 1439 abroad. Malcolm Letts put the old Spanish account into English in 1926.

Tafur visits Constantinople, the Holy Land, Egypt, and the courts of Italy. He notes ships, relics, markets, and the manners of each great city. His eye is curious, shrewd, and often frankly amused by strangers. Few books show the 1400s through one traveler's eyes so well. Readers rank it among the most fun travel works of its century by far. Tafur's voice stays fresh, bold, and plainly human throughout.
journal-of-discourses-vol-26:
Volume Twenty-Six, from 1886, closes the Journal of Discourses for good. Twenty-six volumes span thirty-two years of Tabernacle and frontier preaching. Hundreds of sermons end here, in the set's final gathered book.

The founding generation's voice falls silent as this volume shuts. Apostles who crossed the plains now preach to grandchildren in Zion. Their record covers doctrine, war, law, farming, and the soul's fate. No new faith of the age left so full a firsthand record. Scholars still mine the Journal as Mormonism's great primary source today. Its last pages close an era that print alone could preserve.
holdsworth-history-english-law-vol9-1926:
The ninth volume of Holdsworth's History of English Law came out in 1926, carrying the story toward its author's own time. Holdsworth had begun the history as a young Oxford scholar; by now it was the standard work in its field. Few single-author histories in any subject match its scale.

Volume 9 deals with the later nineteenth century, above all the Judicature Acts that fused the old separate courts into one Supreme Court. Holdsworth explains how law and equity, split for centuries, were at last administered together. The modern court system of England takes its shape in these pages. Nine volumes in, the history approaches its close with the law made new. The set as a whole remains the last word on English legal history for most readers.
bolivian-constitution-1826:
Bolivia's first constitution was adopted in 1826, and it came almost straight from Simón Bolívar's own hand. The Liberator had freed the country that took his name. A congress in Chuquisaca asked him for a charter, and he sent his draft with a famous speech.

The text creates a president who holds office for life, with the right to name his successor. Beside him sit three chambers, including censors charged with guarding morals and the constitution itself. Bolívar argued that a new nation, torn by war, needed a fixed point of authority to survive. Chuquisaca adopted the charter, and Sucre became the first president under it. The lifetime presidency scared many, and the charter lasted only a few years. It remains Bolívar's political last will, written into law.
cia-0000009726:
A Neo Lao Hak Sat weekly bulletin, carrying photographs and details of American prisoners, leads an October 1971 CIA item. Neo Lao Hak Sat was the Pathet Lao's political front in Laos. Its bulletin was propaganda meant for Lao readers, yet it printed real captives' faces.

Enemy publications became unlikely sources for the prisoner accounting. A photograph in a propaganda sheet could prove a man alive and held. Analysts therefore read the other side's press with close, hostile care. This file records that practice: a weekly bulletin mined for names, faces, and dates the enemy never meant to give.
cia-0000009926:
Prison camp bunkers were being built for two American pilots captured in a place the title cuts off, a March 1972 item reports. Bunkers mean digging for permanence and protection from air attack. Captors who build for two named-value prisoners expect to hold them long.

Construction reports revealed the prison system's growth from the ground up. New bunkers also signaled where bombing could endanger the very men it meant to pressure. Officials logged the site for both reasons. This file preserves the building report as received, an entry in the strange architecture of captivity in the war's last year.
cia-0000012426:
The Penkovsky memoirs occupy a CIA paper from May 1963, as the spy's story moves toward print. The colonel was then on trial in Moscow, or just condemned by it. His papers and debriefings were being shaped into a book the agency had a hand in preparing. The file's literary turn had begun while its subject still faced a Soviet court.

The paper weighs the memoir as a publishing proposition, with editors and censors in its future. Such books carried a secret case into public argument. For readers, the memo shows the story's second life being planned before its first life had fully ended.
cia-0000012826:
What could the Soviet Union do, and what would it most likely do, through 1960? A CIA estimate from April 1955 answers both questions at mid-decade. Stalin was two years dead, and his successors were testing new lines abroad while building rockets and bombs at home. The estimate weighs Soviet strength across the board, from divisions to diplomacy.

The mid-fifties balance it strikes set a baseline for a generation of defense planning. It measures the bear's strength at the Cold War's heightening. For readers, the estimate shows the superpower contest being priced, in forces and intentions, by the men charged with knowing.
cia-0000013226:
Viet Cong policy toward American prisoners gets a full study in a CIA paper from September 1969. By then the southern doctrine had years of hard practice behind it. The paper compares the south's rules with Hanoi's rules. It marks the telling differences between the two systems. The south's camps were poorer and more mobile. They were often harsher too, run by cadres closer to the fighting and farther from any capital's control.

The study shows the system's southern face in its own terms. Policy in the jungle answered to local war more than to doctrine. For readers, the paper explains why captivity in the south was its own ordeal.
cia-0000013926: American pilot prisoners were put on parade in Hanoi, in a CIA note dated January 3, 1969. Parading captives through the capital was a show for crowds and cameras. Such displays broke the rules of war as the United States read them. The note records the parade as one more use of prisoners in the public contest.
cia-0000015326: A letter to George Wyllie from Herbert Scoville fills a CIA file dated June 4, 1959. It concerns a book, They Knew Too Much, per the clipped title. Scoville was one of the agency's top science men. A book about spy craft or saucers could pull even him into the mail. The Scoville letter now rests in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015426: The National Investigations Committee on Aerial Phenomena, known as NICAP, is the subject of a redacted CIA case dated January 1, 1965. NICAP was the leading civilian group studying saucer reports in that era. The agency watched its work and kept a case on it. Part of the case was cut before release, leaving the group's name and the date as the firm facts.
cia-0000020326: The private life of Carlos Castillo Armas fills a CIA record dated in 1957. Castillo Armas ruled Guatemala after a 1954 coup backed by the United States. Agencies kept personal files on foreign leaders, habits and all, as part of knowing their man. That the file survives from the year of his death gives it a grim edge for later readers.
cia-0000021526: American pilots held near Ban Na Kay, in Houa Phan Province, died there, a CIA record dated in 1966 reports. Ban Na Kay gives the deaths a place on the map of northeast Laos. No names appear in the title, so the record stands for unnamed men. Such reports closed cases in the worst way and were kept with the same care as hopeful ones.
cia-0000022626: Technical comments on photographs of prisoners of war fill a CIA record dated in 1968. Photo staff judged focus, angle, and detail before matchers trusted a picture. Their notes told other analysts how far a given image could be pushed. Craft remarks like these underpinned the whole comparison effort, where a weak picture could mislead a hopeful search.
cia-0000044426:
A Jesuit priest explained the events leading up to the killings, in a CIA record dated October 5, 1989 in the catalog. He spoke as an insider of the community that was attacked. Few accounts of the case can match a survivor's nearness to it.

Inside, his account walks through the days before the murders. Warnings, fears, and pressures take shape in his telling. Such testimony later mattered to investigators and historians alike. The file preserves the road to the crime as one of its targets lived it. That is the closest view of the case that any reader can get.
cia-0000045926: Diplomats offered views on the photograph said to show American prisoners still held in Southeast Asia. A CIA item dated June 6, 1991, gathered their comments. The picture was then at the center of a fierce public argument over men missing from the Vietnam War. Their careful reactions show governments trying to judge the claim without raising false hope.
cia-0000049226:
Controlling right-wing terrorism in El Salvador is the stated problem of a CIA paper from 1985, preserved in the Truth Commission file series. Four years into the civil war, death squads tied to the far right remained the government's shame and Washington's leverage problem. The paper addresses the question its title asks outright.

Papers of this kind weighed what pressure could do: aid conditions, public naming, and private warnings to the men who protected the squads. They also weighed the risk that pressure would crack the government the aid was meant to save. The paper survives as a record of the dilemma at the center of the war's politics.
cia-0000049326: El Salvador: Politics of Terrorism is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000049326, dated January 5, 1980, marked for the Truth Commission. The paper treats terrorism in El Salvador as a political subject. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
