Secretary William H. Seward directed a letter to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons on 22 May 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d626:
A letter of 30 September 1863, from William H. Seward to William Stuart, stands as document 626 in the printed record. Stuart was Britain's chargé d'affaires in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. Stuart was holding the British legation in Washington while Lord Lyons was away on leave, so the channel ran through him that season.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
plos-pbio-0020126:
Natalay Kouprina, Adam Pavlicek, Ganeshwaran H. Mochida, and their team tracked a brain-size gene in PLOS Biology in 2004. ASPM helps control brain size, and broken copies cause a very small brain at birth. The authors compared ASPM across primates to date its fast evolution.

Their timeline shows the gene's rapid change began before the human brain grew to its modern size. That order matters. It means ASPM was already under strong pressure in earlier primates, not only in our own line. The finding tempers simple stories that tie one gene to one human leap. Brain growth, it hints, was a longer, shared ape story.
plos-pone-0000026:
Ryo Matoba, Hitoshi Niwa, Shinji Masui, and their team profiled embryonic stem cells in PLOS ONE in 2006. The protein Oct3/4 is a master switch that keeps stem cells able to become any cell type. The team measured gene activity as Oct3/4 levels changed, to map the networks it runs.

Lowering the switch lets cells start down paths toward specific tissues. The profiles show which gene groups move first and which hold the stem state. Such maps are the working charts of stem cell biology. They help labs grow pure cell types for study and, in time, for therapy. They also flag genes that might make adult cells revert to a stem-like state.
plos-pone-0000126:
Heidi de Wit, L. Niels Cornelisse, Ruud F. G. Toonen, and colleagues published this neuroscience paper in PLOS ONE in 2006. It studies secretory vesicles, the tiny bubbles inside nerve cells that hold chemical messengers. Before release, a vesicle must dock at the cell surface, and the authors test the role of the protein syntaxin in that step.

Their conclusion is in the title: docking depends on syntaxin. Pinning down which protein does which job matters because every nerve signal rides on this release machinery. The paper adds a precise piece to the chain of events that lets one neuron talk to the next.
plos-pone-0000226:
Stephane Esnault, Ruedi K. Braun, Zhong-Jian Shen, and colleagues published this immunology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Pin1 is an enzyme that tweaks the shape of other proteins after they are made. The authors study how Pin1 modulates the type 1 immune response, the branch of immunity that fights viruses and other invaders inside cells.

A single shape-changing enzyme can tilt the strength of a whole immune program. The paper maps Pin1's influence on that response. Because type 1 responses also drive some inflammatory diseases, the findings matter both for fighting infection and for calming immunity when it overshoots.
plos-pone-0000326:
Rauf Bhat and Carsten Watzl published this immunology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Natural killer cells attack tumor cells without prior training. The authors study serial killing, one killer cell destroying several tumor cells in a row. They report that therapeutic antibodies enhance this serial killing by human natural killer cells.

Antibodies already used in cancer therapy may work partly by coaching killer cells. Showing they boost repeated killing strengthens that account. The finding matters for designing antibody treatments that squeeze the most out of the patient's own immune cells.
plos-pone-0000426:
Jenifer L. Marks and colleagues sequenced growth-signal genes in lung adenocarcinomas, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. They analyzed EGFR and related signaling pathway genes, which drive cell growth and are frequent sources of cancer-causing mutations. Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common form of lung cancer, and its growth genes shape treatment choices.

Alongside known changes, the team identified a novel somatic mutation in the kinase domain of FGFR4, another growth receptor. Somatic means the change arose in the tumor, not in the patient's inherited DNA. Each new mutation of this kind adds a possible drug target and refines how lung tumors are classified at the molecular level.
plos-pone-0000526:
Kegong Tian and colleagues investigated a devastating pig virus outbreak in China, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. PRRS, porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome, took an atypical, fatal turn. The team described the emergence of fatal PRRSV variants and performed molecular dissection of the unique hallmark that set the outbreak strain apart.

A molecular hallmark, a signature change in the virus's genome, lets laboratories identify the dangerous variant quickly. China's 2006–2007 outbreaks killed huge numbers of pigs and shook pork supply. Pinning the variant's distinguishing marks is the first step toward matched vaccines and surveillance.
plos-pone-0000626:
Istvan Molnar-Szakacs, Allan D. Wu, Francisco J. Robles and co-authors asked how brains react to hand gestures from another culture. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study concerns emblems, gestures with fixed meanings that speak without words. People everywhere use their hands to communicate, but each culture sets its own gesture meanings.

The team studied corticospinal excitability, how ready the brain's movement pathways are, while people watched culture-specific gestures. Watching a gesture your own culture taught you may prime your motor system differently from a foreign one. The work speaks to the neural bases of cross-cultural social communication, where a familiar sign can land instantly and an unfamiliar one cannot.
plos-pone-0000726:
Wei Zhao, Bapi Pahar, Juan T. Borda and colleagues tracked immune signals during early infection with a hybrid immunodeficiency virus. The chemokines CCL3, CCL4 and CCL5 can block CCR5-using HIV from entering host cells and suppress viral replication in the lab. What the body's own chemokines do during real infection was incompletely understood.

Their title reports a decline in CCL3-5 gene expression during primary simian-human immunodeficiency virus infection. If natural blockers fall just as the virus establishes itself, that timing could help the virus win. The finding sharpens interest in treatments that sustain or mimic these chemokines during the earliest phase of infection.
plos-pone-0000826:
Abraham Miranda, Meade Morgan, Leda Jamal and colleagues measured whether HIV treatment also slowed tuberculosis in Brazil. HIV fuels TB epidemics around the world. In controlled clinical trials, antiretroviral therapy reduces TB incidence in HIV-infected patients. The open question was whether, under real programmatic conditions, Brazil's policy of universal ART access achieved the same effect between 1995 and 2001.

Trials and national programmes often differ: adherence, supply, and late diagnosis all bite in practice. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study tests the policy at national scale. Evidence that treatment-as-delivered prevents TB strengthens the case for funding universal access, beyond the benefit to each treated patient.
plos-pone-0000926:
Jean-Michel Hougardy, Kinda Schepers, Sammy Place and colleagues tested a blood marker for hidden tuberculosis, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Finding latent TB, infection without illness, is central to controlling the disease. The old skin test misses cases, and newer blood tests rely on the release of a signal protein called interferon gamma.

The team used a TB protein named HBHA to trigger that release. A response to HBHA may mark latent infection more sharply than standard antigens. Better latent tests help doctors treat people before they fall ill or spread the germ. The study adds one more candidate to a busy search.
plos-pone-0001026:
Camila Romano, Fernando de Melo, Marco Corsini and colleagues compared ancient retrovirus families in three primate genomes, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Endogenous retroviruses are old infections written into DNA and passed down. The K family is one of the youngest and most studied of these viral fossils.

The team found nineteen complete ERV-K elements in rhesus monkeys and twelve in chimpanzees, then compared them with fifty-five human copies. Those counts sketch each species' demographic history with the virus family. Viral fossils record infections our ancestors survived. Comparing them across primates shows which copies are shared inheritance and which arrived after the species split.
plos-pone-0001126:
Treating drug-resistant tuberculosis takes many months and often fails. Helen Cox and colleagues reported on a treatment program in Karakalpakstan, Uzbekistan, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The region had very high rates of multidrug-resistant TB, found in 13 percent of new cases and 40 percent of previously treated ones.

A pilot program to treat the disease began there in 2003. The authors describe how treatment worked in practice, what outcomes patients had, and how often extensively drug-resistant TB appeared among those who failed treatment. Their account shows the complexity of curing resistant TB in a high-burden setting.
plos-pone-0001226:
Some lung cancers carry activating mutations in the EGFR gene, and these tumors behave differently from other lung cancers. Kuicheon Choi and colleagues profiled gene activity in such cancer cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The subgroup is non-small cell lung cancer with somatic EGFR mutations, changes acquired by the tumor rather than inherited.

The transcriptional mediators of EGFR's effects in this subgroup had not been fully worked out. Using genetic and pharmacological tools, the authors mapped which genes switch on downstream of the mutant receptor. That map matters because EGFR-blocking drugs work dramatically in this subgroup, and resistance eventually follows.
plos-pone-0001326:
Grapes and wine form a large worldwide market, and the cultivated grape, Vitis vinifera, could become a model for fruit tree genetics. Riccardo Velasco and colleagues produced a draft genome sequence for a heterozygous grapevine variety, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Grapes are highly heterozygous, meaning their two genome copies differ at many positions, which complicates whole-genome shotgun sequencing.

The authors present a high quality draft consensus sequence despite that challenge. A consensus merges the two differing copies into one reference. Their sequence opened grape genomics to gene discovery for disease resistance, fruit quality, and breeding.
plos-pone-0001426:
Peter Kroth and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on sugar handling in a tiny sea alga. Diatoms are single celled algae that fix about a fifth of the world's carbon. Their cells arose through a merged past, so their chemistry is more complex than that of green algae. The team used the full genome to build a model.

Their model maps how this diatom makes, stores, and burns sugars. By comparing it with other algae, they flagged routes that seem unique to diatoms. Those routes may help explain why diatoms thrive in the sea. The model gives labs a base for tests on carbon flow in the oceans.
plos-pone-0001526:
Sophie Desset and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how fruit flies silence jumping DNA in the germ line. Small RNAs guard the genome by hushing these mobile parts. The team studied a locus that directs the hush of two such parts in body cells, not just germ cells. They asked which paths run that hush.

They show the locus works through both a Piwi based path and a second, free path. Two paths to one hush give the cell a backup. Germ line guards keep the next brood's genome sound. This body cell case broadens where such guards are known to act.
plos-pone-0001626:
Koleka Mlisana, Sara C. Auld, Anneke Grobler, and their co-authors measured anaemia in people with very early HIV infection for a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Anaemia, a low level of red blood cells or haemoglobin, is common in AIDS and is linked to worse illness and higher death rates. Far less was known about blood changes in the first weeks of infection with HIV-1 subtype C.

The study followed women who did not yet have HIV alongside women in acute and early infection, tracking how haemoglobin levels changed. The full text gives the blood values, the share of women who became anaemic, and how those patterns shifted over time. Knowing when anaemia starts in early infection can help clinics plan testing and care for people who have just caught the virus.
plos-pone-0001826:
Ke Zen and co-authors identified a molecule that helps breast cancer cells cross vessel walls in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Endothelial E-selectin plays a pivotal role in interactions between breast cancer cells and endothelial monolayers during metastasis. The counterreceptor on the cancer cell, and its role in transendothelial migration, were unknown.

The team reports that CD44v4 is a major E-selectin ligand that mediates breast cancer cell transendothelial migration. The full text gives the binding and migration assays. Metastasis requires cancer cells to exit the bloodstream; blocking the molecular handle they use could slow that step.
plos-pone-0001926:
Hongbo Zhu and co-authors built a new way to compare how proteins touch, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Where two proteins meet, atoms form weak bonds that are not covalent. The pattern of those bonds sets how snug and specific the fit is. Labs had many ways to compare protein shapes and binding sites, but none for these contact patterns.

Their method lines up the weak-bond patterns at two interfaces so like patterns can be scored as alike or not. Aligned in this way, interfaces from unlike proteins can be matched. That helps predict how a new protein will bind, a core task in drug design and in basic cell science.
plos-pone-0002026:
Rongqian Wu and co-authors tested a hunger hormone as a shield against gut injury, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. When blood flow to the gut is cut and then restored, a pattern called ischemia-reperfusion, the harm can spread from the gut to distant organs. Immune cells along the gut's vast vessel surface drive a local, then body-wide, inflammatory response.

The hormone is ghrelin, best known for sparking appetite. As the title states, ghrelin attenuated injury both in the gut and in remote organs after this insult. A gut hormone that also calms storm-like injury could aid care in intensive units.
plos-pone-0002126:
David Hendrickson, Daniel Hogan, Daniel Herschlag, and co-authors mapped how tiny RNAs steer gene activity, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. MicroRNAs are short pieces of RNA that do not code for proteins. Instead, they guide a silencing complex to matching messenger RNAs, which can then be cut down or blocked from making protein.

The team set out to find, in a systematic way, which messenger RNAs one protein pulls in. That protein is Argonaute 2, and the search ran when a given microRNA was at work. They also tracked how the amounts of those messages change. Their approach helps replace guesswork about microRNA targets with direct lists drawn from cells.
plos-pone-0002226:
Nikolaus Steinbeis and Stefan Koelsch compared how the brain handles meaning in music and in language, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Music can plainly carry meaning, yet how it does so is unsettled. The team asked whether the meaning of a musical passage is represented in the brain much as the meaning of a sentence is.

They combined EEG, which times brain activity finely, with fMRI, which locates it. The two methods together gave evidence for neural representations that are partly shared and partly distinct. The study helps map where music and language meet in the mind, and where each keeps its own machinery.
plos-pone-0002326:
Christian Dobel, Christian Putsche, Pienie Zwitserlood, and co-authors recorded brain signals from people born unable to recognize faces, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Congenital prosopagnosia is a severe face perception problem present from birth, not caused by injury. People with it cannot recognize even familiar persons by face.

Using MEG, which tracks magnetic fields from the brain with fine timing, the team looked for early faults in face processing. They found dysfunction in the left hemisphere at early stages. A fault that early suggests the problem starts in the first steps of face analysis. It does not start in memory for people. That reshapes how the condition is classed.
plos-pone-0002426:
Work from Llop-Guevara and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Alba Llop-Guevara, Marc Colangelo, Derek K. Chu, and others. Its subject is in Vivo -to- In Silico Iterations to Investigate Aeroallergen-Host Interactions. Allergic asthma is a complex process arising out of the interaction between the immune system and aeroallergens.

Yet, the relationship between aeroallergen exposure, allergic sensitization and disease remains unclear. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002526:
In 2008, Wei and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Bin Wei, Zheng Chen, Xu Zhang, and others. Its subject is nitric Oxide Mediates Stretch-Induced Ca2+ Release via Activation of Phosphatidylinositol 3-Kinase-Akt Pathway in Smooth Muscle. Hollow smooth muscle organs such as the bladder undergo significant changes in wall tension linked to filling and distension.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002626:
Michael Klompas led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was automated identification of acute hepatitis b using electronic medical record data to facilitate public health surveillance. The catalog record names Michael Klompas first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Automatic identification of notifiable diseases from electronic medical records can potentially improve the timeliness and completeness of public health surveillance. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002726:
Rajkumar Sasidharan led a team whose 2008 PLOS ONE article deals with transmembrane protein oxygen content and compartmentalization of cells. Authorship is credited in the record to Rajkumar Sasidharan and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Recently. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state. The description here rests only on the title, the author record, and the abstract text held for the entry, with no claims added beyond those sources.
plos-pone-0002826:
Jenee N. Smith led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was SdiA, an n -Acylhomoserine lactone receptor, becomes active during the transit of salmonella enterica through the gastrointestinal tract of turtles. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Jenee N. Smith, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. LuxR-type transcription factors are typically used by bacteria to determine the population density of their own species by detecting N-acylhomoserine lactones (AHLs). Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002926:
Maria Camats, Sonia Guil, Mariette Kokolo and co-authors studied how the helicase p68 shapes H-Ras splicing in 2008. H-Ras RNA can be spliced two ways, making either the p21 or the p19 protein, depending on whether a piece called IDX is kept. The p68 protein was known to reduce IDX inclusion.

Published in PLOS ONE, the study shows p68 also alters the activity of other splicing factors that act on the same RNA. Splicing is how one gene yields several proteins. The results add detail on how a single helicase can steer that choice in a cancer-linked gene.
plos-pone-0003026: Stephen Beres, Ricardo Sesso, Sergio Pinto and colleagues reported the genome sequence of a Lancefield group C Streptococcus zooepidemicus strain in PLOS ONE in 2008. The strain caused epidemic nephritis, a kidney disease outbreak, and the subtitle calls the work new information about an old disease. The catalog record gives title, authors, and year, with no further abstract detail. The article presents the full genome of that outbreak strain as a base for studying how this animal-associated streptococcus infects people.
plos-pone-0003126:
Yara C. Blanco, Alessandro S. Farias, Uta Goelnitz and co-authors test a support treatment for cerebral malaria in this 2008 PLOS ONE study. Cerebral malaria brings nerve signs, seizures and coma, and it shares some traits with stroke. Even so, few studies had looked at new supportive care for the disease. Hyperbaric oxygen, given under pressure, had shown success in other settings.

The title states the central finding: hyperbaric oxygen prevented early death in mice with experimental cerebral malaria. Readers find a test of a non-drug support idea for a severe form of malaria. The work points to care that might buy time alongside standard treatment.
plos-pone-0003226:
Kwok M. Ho, Matthew Knuiman, Judith Finn and colleagues build a survival model for critically ill patients in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Long-term survival outcome of critically ill patients is important for assessing new treatments and for making treatment decisions. The team developed a prognostic model for estimation of long-term survival, called PREDICT. It was a retrospective linked data cohort study.

Readers get a tool aimed beyond hospital discharge, at long-term outlook. Families and clinicians often need that longer view when weighing intensive care. A validated model can support those hard conversations with data instead of guesswork alone.
plos-pone-0003326:
Scot E. Dowd, Randall D. Wolcott, Yan Sun and colleagues sequence bacteria from diabetic foot ulcers in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Ulcers on the feet and legs of people with diabetes are linked with chronic infections. Such ulcer infections are too often followed by amputation. There is little knowledge of the ecology of such infections, or of how to control or clear this type of chronic infection.

Using bacterial tag encoded FLX amplicon pyrosequencing, the team show the polymicrobial nature of chronic diabetic foot ulcer biofilm infections. Readers learn these wounds host mixed groups, not single germs. That mix explains why antibiotics aimed at one species often fail in such ulcers.
plos-pone-0007426: Flu epidemics return year after year, and this study asks why: is the virus changing steadily, or in sudden jumps? Using simple mathematical models of evolution, the researchers tested whether the virus's main surface protein changes gradually or in bursts. The models favored a punctuated pattern — long calm stretches broken by leaps — which helps explain how flu keeps slipping past immunity.
plos-pone-0007526: Even in E. coli, the most studied bacterium on Earth, most of the starting points where gene reading begins were unknown. This study mapped transcription start sites, promoters, and regulator binding sites across the whole genome. The completed map fills a major gap in our understanding of how this model organism controls its genes.
plos-pone-0007626: The dome-headed dinosaur Pachycephalosaurus changed so dramatically as it grew that juveniles and adults look like different species. This study of its skull development revealed extreme late-stage growth spurts. The work warns paleontologists that some 'new species' may just be teenagers.
plos-pone-0007726: Diabetes drugs of the TZD class and a related prostaglandin both calm the immune system, but their effects on gamma-delta T cells were unknown. This study tested both on human Vδ2 T cells involved in autoimmunity. The results clarify how these metabolic drugs modulate an overlooked immune player.
plos-pone-0007826: Childhood leukemia got a tiny-RNA crystal ball. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Zhang's team linked microRNA patterns to prognosis and brain relapse in kids' leukemia. Adult clues did not carry over. The pattern links were mapped. The crystal ball feeds pediatric oncology.
plos-pone-0007926: Family liver failure got a telomere-gene link. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Calado's team tied severe inherited liver disease to telomerase faults. Short telomeres hit busy cells hardest. The mutation list was mapped. The link feeds liver medicine.
plos-pone-0008026: Stubborn cancer cells got an antibody Hail Mary. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Gougelet's team tested anti-IL-6 against treatment-resistant cancer cells. High IL-6 tracks with resistance. The Hail Mary fell short. The test tempers antibody hopes.
plos-pone-0008126: Drug side effects were predicted from gene activity over time. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Huang and colleagues forecast pharmacological and xenobiotic responses from time-course gene expression profiles. Late-stage side effects kill promising drugs. The early-warning system spots trouble from how genes react in the first hours.
plos-pone-0008226: Gut pain was tied to overactive immune sensors. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by McKernan's team found extra Toll-like receptor messages in the colons of two animal models of irritable bowel syndrome. Stress is thought to scramble brain-gut-immune chatter in IBS. The heightened sensors suggest the gut's alarm system is stuck on. The finding points to immune-calming strategies for the wrenching disorder.
plos-pone-0008326: Night-dwelling mammals were found tuning their vision genes. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Zhao's team traced rhodopsin evolution in mammals living in dim light. Eyes adapt to light worlds through anatomy and through the visual proteins themselves. The team read rhodopsin genes across species. The molecular changes show how evolution rewired night vision again and again.
plos-pone-0008426: A pig germ's hairs got a parts list. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Fittipaldi's team showed mutations in the ancillary pilin leave Streptococcus suis pili built from the major subunit alone. The hair-like structures aid virulence. The minimal pili still formed. The parts list informs anti-virulence strategies.
plos-pone-0008526: A cancer virus got a triple disguise. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Tang's team derived a triple-mosaic adenovirus for cancer gene therapy. The chimeric vector dodges immunity better. The mosaic design broadens targeting while slipping past defenses. The triple threat advances cancer virotherapy.
plos-pone-0008626: Alzheimer's toxicity got a fly-tested brake. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Sanokawa-Akakura's team showed FKBP52 and copper balance control amyloid-beta toxicity in Drosophila. The immunophilin's protective role was decoded. The copper link was mapped. The fly test nominates a therapy angle.
plos-pone-0008726: Tumor-cell squeezing got measured. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Rolli's team used microchannels to link tumor-cell cytoskeleton organization to invasiveness and migration. The stiffness-deformation trade was mapped. The measure informs metastasis science.
plos-pone-0008826: A dopamine-making enzyme got its portrait. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Han's team solved the crystal structure of Drosophila DDC and mapped its substrate specificity. The decarboxylase's active site was decoded. The portrait informs neurochemistry.
plos-pone-0008926: Cow-burp gas got a germ blueprint. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Leahy's team read the full code of a cow-gut methane germ. The gas-maker's blueprint was mapped gene by gene. The blueprint hints at burp-cutting fixes.
plos-pone-0009026: Fat stem cells got a reprogramming recipe. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Jee's team used a DHP-derivative plus low oxygen to reprogram human adipose stromal cells. The dedifferentiation cocktail was validated. The recipe aids regenerative medicine.
plos-pone-0009126: Gabon's Ebola immunity got a survey. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Becquart's team found high humoral and cellular immunity to Zaire ebolavirus among rural Gabonese. The 4,349-person serosurvey was run. The survey informs Ebola ecology.
plos-pone-0009226: A cell-swallowing switch got a delayed feedback. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Zhu's team showed Rab5's positive feedback by Rabex-5 and Rabaptin-5 has a delayed onset. The endocytosis timing was mapped. The delay informs cell biology.
plos-pone-0009326: DNA's corkscrew got a twist logic. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Timsit and Várnai tied DNA's corkscrew to its overall knot shape. The twist logic was modeled. The logic feeds DNA physics. The logic spans scales and functions.
plos-pone-0011426: Even genetically identical worms differ from one another, and measuring that variation is tricky. This research paper quantifies the differences in isogenic C. elegans using a glowing stress reporter, hsp-16.2 linked to GFP, clustered into two-dimensional patterns. The method turns worm-to-worm variation into hard numbers, giving biologists a sharper tool for studying nature versus nurture at the single-gene level.
plos-pone-0011526: Muscles contract when calcium floods out of storage, released through ryanodine receptor channels. This research paper compares the alpha and beta ryanodine receptors of frogs in a muscle cell line and finds they produce distinct calcium signals. The two-channel system shows how one cell can tune its calcium messages with fine control.
plos-pone-0011626: Flu tracking needs daily local alarms, not weekly national averages. This research paper builds a math model that watches flu-like illness reports day by day, town by town. The system flags outbreaks sooner, giving local health teams a head start on response.
plos-pone-0011726: Calming immune cells called regulatory T cells could treat autoimmunity if aimed at the right targets. This research paper builds human Tregs with chosen targets by moving T-cell receptor genes into them. The custom-built peacekeepers point toward tailored immune therapy.
plos-pone-0011826: Bird flu's H5N1 strain kills with frightening power, once blamed on a single protein snip. This research paper finds more virulence factors beyond that famous cleavage site. The added culprits complete the portrait of what makes this flu so deadly.
plos-pone-0011926: Trial abstracts shape medical practice — but are they reported well? This research paper assesses reporting quality in abstracts of randomized trials across five leading Chinese medical journals. The audit exposes gaps between the abstracts and the full story within the paper.
plos-pone-0012026: The 17β-HSD1 enzyme shapes estrogen — and drug designers want its secrets. This research paper probes its kinetics and ligand binding through dynamic motion studies. The moving picture of the enzyme reveals how it grabs its targets in action in the body.
plos-pone-0012126: The bacterium that makes erythromycin hides teamwork among its genes. This research paper maps groups of genes that switch on together in Saccharopolyspora erythraea over time. The teamwork map reveals the antibiotic factory's hidden control logic today, tomorrow, and always.
plos-pone-0012226: A blood enzyme flags fatty liver disease in insulin-resistant patients. This research paper studies serum DPP-4 activity in insulin resistant patients with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease as a novel liver disease biomarker. The DPP-4 biomarker aids early liver disease detection, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all.
plos-pone-0012326: Williams syndrome brains hear wholes, not parts. This research paper shows the left-leaning auditory cortex drives whole-sound hearing in Williams syndrome. The left-leaning finding reveals odd sound wiring, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012426: Do doctors carry communication skills from rounds to the ward? This research paper studies transfer of communication skills to the workplace during clinical rounds and the impact of a program for residents. The transfer findings inform medical training, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012526: PolyADP-ribosylation glues pronuclei together after mating. This research paper shows polyADP-ribosylation is required for nucleus fusion after mating in mice. The fusion requirement reveals a fertility step, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012626: Cofilin-1 loss floods kidneys with protein. This research paper shows cofilin-1 inactivation leads to proteinuria, studied in zebrafish, mice and humans. The cofilin-1 finding reveals a kidney-filter gene, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012726: One 35-gene signature types and forecasts B-cell lymphoma. The Quest of the Holy Grail is W. W. Comfort's 1926 English version of the Queste del Saint Graal. That French text formed part of the vast Vulgate cycle of Arthurian romance. Its mood is stern and monastic, quite unlike the lighter tales of Arthur's court.

The Free-Masons Accusation and Defence, printed in London in 1726, gathers six genuine letters for and against the Craft. It is the earliest printed controversy over Freemasonry.
